messages.author: 6bc640c9f98380b3
messages.subject: exact.matches time trials
parts:
This is not a question as such, just sharing my own experience of Stefan's exact.matches() script..

I found quite a difference in the time  exact.matches() takes to run when the "characters.around" argument is added. Compare the following times, based on a corpus vector of about 56,000 sentences of the 500 Brown XML files. By contrast, there was no great difference in time when the "lines.around" argument is added.


# no characters.around argument
> start <-Sys.time()
> results_allchars <- exact.matches("too", brown.sentences.500)
> end <-Sys.time()
> (end-start)

Time difference of 0.5530379 secs

> length(results[[4]])
[1] 1689


# with characters.around argument
> start <-Sys.time()
> results_10chars <- exact.matches("too", brown.sentences.500, characters.around = 10)
> end <-Sys.time()
> (end-start)

Time difference of 2.011826 mins

> length(results_10chars[[4]])
[1] 1689


# with lines.around argument
> results_2lines = vector()
> start <-Sys.time()
> results_2lines <- exact.matches("too", brown.sentences.500, lines.around = 2)
> end <-Sys.time()
> (end-start)

Time difference of 0.722476 secs

> length(results_2lines[[4]])
[1] 1689

So, adding the argument to restrict context to 10 characters around the node word takes you from about 0.5 secs to 2 minutes. I think it may have something to do with the subroutine in exact.matches() which collapses all the components of the original corpus.vector into a single string (over 25 million characters long in this case) when characters.around kicks in with some number other than 0. My own way around this is to use a loop so that the collapsed corpus.vector is never more than a sentence long.

> results_10chars = vector()
> start <-Sys.time()
> for (i in 1:length(brown.sentences.500)) {
+ current.matches <- exact.matches("too", brown.sentences.500[i], characters.around = 10)[[4]]
+ results_10chars <- append(results_10chars, current.matches)
+ }
> end <-Sys.time()
> (end-start)

Time difference of 3.64961 secs

> length(results_10chars)
[1] 1689

John

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] exact.matches time trials
parts: > I think it may have something to do with the subroutine in exact.matches() which collapses all the components of the original corpus.vector into a single string (over 25 million characters long in this case) when characters.around kicks in

Definitely, yes. After all, there is one paste operation going on for
the whole corpus.vector, and then a gsub again on the whole corpus
plus at that time the very long corpus vector is also kinda
'reduplicated' in memory as lines.with.matches.

I do know how it could be fixed: one would

- never conflate the whole corpus but do something like
nchar(corpus.vector) early in the script so that one knows all the
character lengths of all elements of corpus.vector;
- then, on the basis of that info, conflate only as many lines as
needed but never the whole corpus.

However, since

- I never use it - if anything, I use lines.around and
- the characters.around option is only in there for kicks and
'historical fun' to provide this as old corpus software did,

this fix will have to wait till a the rare confluence of me having a
transoceanic flight AND no reviewing to do ;-) But: exact.matches is
open 'software' so if anyone needs this now, please, feel free to use
the above hints as to how to do it and, ideally, post your experience
here, too. exact.matches can only get better :-)

Cheers and many thanks, John, for testing AND reporting back!!
